title: If one teammate wins, does the whole team win?
answer: Yes. A successful win condition for either teammate wins the game for both teammates.
explanation: Yes. A successful win condition for either teammate wins the game for both teammates.
example: Your Approach of the Second Sun resolves from your hand after you previously cast another spell with that name this game. If its win instruction succeeds, you and your teammate win together.
exceptions: A can’t-win restriction can stop an alternative win. If a player would win and lose simultaneously, CR 104.3f gives the loss precedence.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: If one teammate loses, can the other keep playing?
answer: No. Either teammate losing eliminates the whole team, even if the other player has a healthy library and useful permanents.
explanation: No. Either teammate losing eliminates the whole team, even if the other player has a healthy library and useful permanents.
example: Phage enters under your control after you cast her from the command zone, not your hand. If her lose-the-game trigger resolves without protection, both teammates lose.
exceptions: A relevant can’t-lose effect can prevent a loss; concession follows its own rule.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Does milling one opponent cause both teammates to lose?
answer: An empty library alone does not cause a loss. When that opponent subsequently attempts an unreplaced draw from the empty library, the loss at the next state-based-action check eliminates their entire team.
explanation: An empty library alone does not cause a loss. When that opponent subsequently attempts an unreplaced draw from the empty library, the loss at the next state-based-action check eliminates their entire team.
example: You mill the last 12 cards from one opponent. Both opponents remain in the game. A later instruction makes that player draw a card from their empty library; their team then loses when state-based actions are checked.
exceptions: A draw replacement or a can’t-lose effect may change the outcome. Milling is not the same action as drawing.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Do I lose for drawing the last card in my library?
answer: No. Drawing the last available card succeeds. A later draw attempt with no card available is the problem.
explanation: No. Drawing the last available card succeeds. A later draw attempt with no card available is the problem.
example: Your library contains one card. You draw it in the shared draw step and now have an empty library. That successful draw does not make your team lose.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: What if a draw instruction asks for more cards than remain?
answer: Draw as many cards as are available, one at a time. An unfulfilled draw from the empty library causes a loss at the next state-based-action check, rather than stopping the resolving spell at that moment.
explanation: Draw as many cards as are available, one at a time. An unfulfilled draw from the empty library causes a loss at the next state-based-action check, rather than stopping the resolving spell at that moment.
example: An instruction says draw three cards, but you have two. You draw those two and fail the third draw. Finish resolving that spell or ability; absent a replacement or protection, your team loses before a player next receives priority.
exceptions: If an empty-library draw is replaced by a win, that win can instead end the game immediately.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Can my teammate’s library supply a card for my draw?
answer: No. Each player draws from their own library. Sharing a draw step does not combine libraries or let one teammate draw for the other.
explanation: No. Each player draws from their own library. Sharing a draw step does not combine libraries or let one teammate draw for the other.
example: You have no cards in your library and your teammate has 50. During an ordinary team draw step you each draw your own card. Your failed draw still threatens the whole team.
exceptions: An effect that skips or replaces your draw must be applied before assuming a failed draw occurs.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Can I respond after a failed draw to avoid losing?
answer: You cannot respond to the state-based loss. Protect yourself, replace the draw, or put a card into the library before the draw instruction resolves.
explanation: You cannot respond to the state-based loss. Protect yourself, replace the draw, or put a card into the library before the draw instruction resolves.
example: A draw spell is on the stack and your library is empty. You may respond with a suitable instant before it resolves. Once it resolves and an unreplaced empty draw occurs, ordinary priority does not provide a rescue window before the loss check.
exceptions: State-based actions wait until the resolving spell or ability finishes. A relevant replacement or effect within that resolution can matter.
Refilling the library after the failed draw does not erase that attempt; the next loss check still sees it.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Can Laboratory Maniac win the game for both teammates?
answer: Yes, if its controller would draw from their own empty library and its replacement effect applies. That individual win becomes a team win.
explanation: Yes, if its controller would draw from their own empty library and its replacement effect applies. That individual win becomes a team win.
example: You control Laboratory Maniac, have an empty library, and resolve a draw effect. Its replacement turns your draw into a win for your team. Your teammate having an empty library instead does not satisfy your Maniac.
exceptions: The Maniac must be present when the draw would happen. An opponent can remove it before the draw resolves; can’t-win effects also matter.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Does Thassa’s Oracle check both teammates’ libraries?
answer: No. It checks its ability controller’s devotion and library. If that ability produces a win, the win applies to the whole team.
explanation: No. It checks its ability controller’s devotion and library. If that ability produces a win, the win applies to the whole team.
example: You control Oracle and its trigger. Your library is empty, so even devotion zero is enough when the trigger checks. Your teammate’s 80-card library does not prevent your team from winning.
exceptions: Your teammate’s empty library does not help your own Oracle check. Changing your library or applying a can’t-win effect before resolution may prevent the win.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: When does a team lose for zero or negative life?
answer: The shared life total being zero or lower causes a loss when state-based actions are checked. There is no separate positive life total for the other teammate.
explanation: The shared life total being zero or lower causes a loss when state-based actions are checked. There is no separate positive life total for the other teammate.
example: Your team has 5 life. An opponent makes one teammate lose 6 life. The shared total becomes −1, and the team loses at the next state-based-action check unless an applicable protection prevents it.
exceptions: A can’t-lose effect may prevent the loss. Life can briefly fall below zero and be restored during one resolving spell before the check.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Can I pay our shared life total all the way down to zero?
answer: A legal life payment may equal the shared life total, but that usually makes your team lose at the next state-based-action check. You cannot pay more life than your team has.
explanation: A legal life payment may equal the shared life total, but that usually makes your team lose at the next state-based-action check. You cannot pay more life than your team has.
example: At exactly 50 shared life, you can pay 50 to activate Aetherflux Reservoir. Without protection or another applicable effect, your team loses before the damage ability resolves.
exceptions: Restrictions on paying or losing life can forbid a payment. Separate simultaneous payments cannot collectively exceed the shared total.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Can one commander’s combat damage eliminate the whole team?
answer: Yes. If one player has received 21 or more combat damage from the same commander over the game, that player’s loss eliminates their team even if its shared life total is positive.
explanation: Yes. If one player has received 21 or more combat damage from the same commander over the game, that player’s loss eliminates their team even if its shared life total is positive.
example: The same commander hits you for 11 combat damage and later 10 more. You have received 21 from that commander, so your team loses at the state-based-action check.
exceptions: Only combat damage counts. The CR describes a recipient player, while the official 2HG overview uses broader team wording. This FAQ does not settle the existing split-recipient aggregation question; check the organizer’s published clarification rather than assuming 11 to one head plus 10 to the other.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Do damage totals from different commanders combine for a commander-damage loss?
answer: No. Track each commander separately. Different commanders do not combine into one 21-damage total.
explanation: No. Track each commander separately. Different commanders do not combine into one 21-damage total.
example: One opposing commander has dealt you 12 combat damage and the other has dealt you 12. That is 24 damage toward shared life, but neither individual commander has reached 21 against you.
exceptions: A commander can still deal ordinary damage that reduces shared life to zero. Changing that commander’s controller does not reset its accumulated commander damage.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Is poison counted as ten per player or fifteen per team?
answer: Two-Headed Giant uses a shared team poison total. Fifteen or more poison counters causes the team to lose at a state-based-action check; the ordinary ten-poison player threshold does not apply.
explanation: Two-Headed Giant uses a shared team poison total. Fifteen or more poison counters causes the team to lose at a state-based-action check; the ordinary ten-poison player threshold does not apply.
example: Your team has 8 poison counters. One teammate receives 4 more and the other receives 3 more. The shared total is 15, so your team loses.
exceptions: An applicable can’t-lose effect may prevent this loss. This is separate from life total.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Does gaining life erase poison or commander damage?
answer: No. Life gain changes the shared life total, not poison counters or the history of combat damage dealt by a commander.
explanation: No. Life gain changes the shared life total, not poison counters or the history of combat damage dealt by a commander.
example: You have received 20 combat damage from a commander and then your team gains 30 life. One more combat damage from that same commander to you still reaches 21.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Can I concede without eliminating my teammate?
answer: No. One teammate conceding makes the team leave immediately. A can’t-lose effect does not force someone to remain in the game.
explanation: No. One teammate conceding makes the team leave immediately. A can’t-lose effect does not force someone to remain in the game.
example: You control Platinum Angel but decide to concede. Your teammate cannot continue the game alone; your entire team leaves and loses.
exceptions: Tournament conduct, penalties and match procedures are administered separately by the organizer or judge.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Does one Platinum Angel protect both teammates from losing?
answer: Yes. In 2HG, a player’s can’t-lose restriction protects that player’s team, and a player’s opponents being unable to win restricts the opposing team.
explanation: Yes. In 2HG, a player’s can’t-lose restriction protects that player’s team, and a player’s opponents being unable to win restricts the opposing team.
example: You control Platinum Angel and your teammate attempts to draw from an empty library. The Angel’s can’t-lose effect prevents your team’s resulting loss while it remains active.
exceptions: This does not prevent damage, life loss, poison counters or failed draws. Concession still works. Removing the Angel can expose a continuing zero-life or fifteen-poison condition; an old protected failed draw is not a permanently queued loss.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Does a restriction saying I can’t win also restrict my teammate?
answer: Yes. An effect saying a player can’t win also prevents that player’s team from winning through a win effect.
explanation: Yes. An effect saying a player can’t win also prevents that player’s team from winning through a win effect.
example: You control Abyssal Persecutor. Even if your teammate resolves a normally successful Thassa’s Oracle trigger, your team cannot win through that effect while the restriction applies.
exceptions: Concession and all-opponents-leaving rules are separate from trying to resolve an alternative win condition.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Does “you can’t lose the game” prevent damage or life loss?
answer: No. Losing life and losing the game are different events. A team can have zero or negative life while protected from losing the game.
explanation: No. Losing life and losing the game are different events. A team can have zero or negative life while protected from losing the game.
example: With Platinum Angel protecting your team at 3 life, a teammate loses 5 life. Your shared total becomes −2. The Angel prevents the loss, not the life change; if it leaves while the total is still −2, the next check is fatal.
exceptions: Effects saying life totals can’t change or life can’t be lost are different restrictions.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Does a can’t-lose effect by itself stop an opponent’s alternative win?
answer: No. Preventing your team from losing does not by itself prevent the opposing team from winning. A separate can’t-win restriction is needed.
explanation: No. Preventing your team from losing does not by itself prevent the opposing team from winning. A separate can’t-win restriction is needed.
example: Lich’s Mastery protects your team from losing. An opponent’s successful Thassa’s Oracle win can still end the game because Mastery does not say opponents can’t win.
exceptions: Platinum Angel has both relevant restrictions, so its result differs from a card that only says you can’t lose.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Does Angel’s Grace protect my teammate from losing this turn?
answer: Its can’t-lose and opponents-can’t-win clauses protect your team for the turn. Its damage-to-you clause does not automatically protect damage dealt to your teammate.
explanation: Its can’t-lose and opponents-can’t-win clauses protect your team for the turn. Its damage-to-you clause does not automatically protect damage dealt to your teammate.
example: You resolve Angel’s Grace before your teammate’s unpaid Pact trigger resolves. The team is protected from that loss event for the turn. Do not assume the spell also makes all damage to your teammate leave your team at 1 life.
exceptions: Its split second does not counter spells or abilities already on the stack. Detailed teammate-damage calculations remain subject to their own source analysis.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Does temporary protection queue every prevented loss for later?
answer: No. A one-time lose-the-game instruction that fails under protection is not automatically repeated later. An ongoing lethal life or poison condition is checked again after protection expires.
explanation: No. A one-time lose-the-game instruction that fails under protection is not automatically repeated later. An ongoing lethal life or poison condition is checked again after protection expires.
example: Angel’s Grace stops an unpaid Pact’s lose-the-game instruction. That specific instruction does not retry next turn. But if your team is still at zero life when Grace expires, the next state-based-action check can make your team lose.
exceptions: Another failed draw after protection ends can create a new loss. Protection is not permission to ignore future required payments.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Does Teferi’s Protection stop every way our team can lose?
answer: No. Its life-total restriction protects the shared life total, but its protection applies to its controller. It does not say the team can’t lose.
explanation: No. Its life-total restriction protects the shared life total, but its protection applies to its controller. It does not say the team can’t lose.
example: While you are protected, an opponent can still make your unprotected teammate draw from an empty library. Their resulting loss still eliminates your team. Targeting restrictions and draw replacements must be checked separately.
exceptions: It does not erase poison counters or commander-damage history. Phasing out your permanents does not phase out your teammate’s permanents.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Does one teammate’s unpaid Pact cause a team loss?
answer: Yes. If that player’s Pact payment is not made and its lose instruction succeeds, the entire team loses. The other teammate’s mana pool cannot pay that cost.
explanation: Yes. If that player’s Pact payment is not made and its lose instruction succeeds, the entire team loses. The other teammate’s mana pool cannot pay that cost.
example: Your Pact of Negation upkeep trigger resolves and you cannot pay its required mana. Your teammate has enough untapped lands, but their mana is not yours. Unless a relevant effect prevents the loss, both teammates lose.
exceptions: A specifically applicable mana-granting effect or can’t-lose effect can change the result; merely sharing a turn does not.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Do extra-turn spells also expose the whole team to their delayed loss?
answer: Yes. A granted extra turn is a team turn. If the spell later makes its controller lose and that instruction succeeds, both teammates lose.
explanation: Yes. A granted extra turn is a team turn. If the spell later makes its controller lose and that instruction succeeds, both teammates lose.
example: You resolve Final Fortune. Both teammates take the extra turn. At that turn’s end step its delayed trigger tells you to lose; if it resolves without protection, your entire team loses.
exceptions: Countering or otherwise stopping a delayed trigger is different from removing a permanent. The ability’s actual wording and timing matter.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Can “target player loses the game” eliminate a team with 60 life?
answer: Yes. A successful explicit lose-the-game effect on one opponent eliminates that opponent’s team regardless of shared life.
explanation: Yes. A successful explicit lose-the-game effect on one opponent eliminates that opponent’s team regardless of shared life.
example: Door to Nothingness targets one opposing player. If its ability resolves and the loss is not prevented, both opposing teammates lose even at 60 shared life.
exceptions: The ability must have a legal target and can be disrupted. Relevant can’t-lose restrictions still apply.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Can a starting 60 life total satisfy Test of Endurance or Felidar Sovereign?
answer: Yes. A life-total check for either teammate uses the shared total. Their upkeep triggers still need their stated conditions when triggering and when resolving; they do not win during setup.
explanation: Yes. A life-total check for either teammate uses the shared total. Their upkeep triggers still need their stated conditions when triggering and when resolving; they do not win during setup.
example: You control Test of Endurance and begin your upkeep at 60 shared life, satisfying its 50-life threshold. If your team falls to 49 before the trigger resolves, that trigger does not win the game.
exceptions: Felidar’s threshold is 40 rather than 50. Countering the trigger or a can’t-win effect can prevent a win.
Removing the permanent before upkeep prevents its trigger. Removing it after the trigger exists does not by itself stop that ability.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Does one Aetherflux Reservoir activation eliminate a team at 60 life?
answer: Normally no. It deals 50 damage to one targeted opponent, reducing the opposing shared total from 60 to 10. Your own 50-life payment also reduces your shared life total.
explanation: Normally no. It deals 50 damage to one targeted opponent, reducing the opposing shared total from 60 to 10. Your own 50-life payment also reduces your shared life total.
example: Both teams are at 60. You pay 50, leaving your team at 10, then the ability deals 50 to one opponent, leaving that team at 10 too.
exceptions: Prevention, replacement effects or damage modifiers can change the arithmetic. Paying from exactly 50 is dangerous because your team reaches zero before resolution.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Does Sorin Markov set just one head to 10 while the other keeps 60?
answer: No. Setting one player’s life total changes the shared total to the specified value. There is no second independent life total to preserve.
explanation: No. Setting one player’s life total changes the shared total to the specified value. There is no second independent life total to preserve.
example: The opposing team is at 60. Sorin’s −3 sets one opponent’s life to 10. That player loses 50 life, so the shared team total becomes 10.
exceptions: Effects preventing or replacing life changes must be considered. An effect setting every player’s total uses different 2HG instructions under CR 810.9d.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: What happens if both teams lose at the same time?
answer: If all remaining teams lose simultaneously, the game is a draw.
explanation: If all remaining teams lose simultaneously, the game is a draw.
example: Both teams have 4 life. Earthquake with X = 2 deals 2 damage to each of the four players, reducing each shared total by 4. If nothing prevents a loss, both teams reach zero together and the next state-based-action check produces a draw.
exceptions: A team protected from losing may survive while the other loses. Separate triggers resolving one after another are not automatically simultaneous.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Can a life-gain trigger save us after lethal damage?
answer: A trigger waiting to go on the stack does not resolve before state-based actions. A team already at zero or less usually loses before that trigger can save it.
explanation: A trigger waiting to go on the stack does not resolve before state-based actions. A team already at zero or less usually loses before that trigger can save it.
example: A resolved effect leaves your team at −2 and causes an ability that will gain 5 life to trigger. Without protection, the team loses before that waiting life-gain ability is put on the stack and resolves.
exceptions: Life gained during the same resolving spell or ability can restore a positive total before the check. Gaining life before the damage resolves can also work.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Are all infinite combos automatic draws?
answer: No. A loop containing only mandatory actions can draw the game. An optional repeatable combo does not become a draw merely because a player calls it infinite.
explanation: No. A compulsory loop that cannot be stopped can draw the game under the loop rules. An optional repeatable combo does not become a draw merely because a player calls it infinite.
example: A player can choose whether to activate a repeatable mana ability again. That is an optional loop: propose a finite number of iterations and a resulting game state rather than declaring the game drawn.
exceptions: This FAQ does not add a combo ban, turn restriction or tournament slow-play policy. A judge or organizer may need to supervise a disputed loop.
Players are not forced to spend an unrelated removal spell or take another outside action to break a mandatory loop.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.
